cards.hook: Under uncertainty, beliefs are numbers between 0 (certainly false) and 1 (certainly true).

example: Medical diagnosis: hidden disease state + false positive tests → partially observable AND treatment effects are non-deterministic.
cards.memory: OR adds, AND multiplies, NOT subtracts from 1, GIVEN divides.
cards.trap: Adding only works for MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE events; multiplying only for INDEPENDENT events.
explain: Probability is a number from 0 (certainly false) to 1 (certainly true) expressing how strongly you believe something.

NOT: 1 − P. OR for events that can't happen together: add. AND for independent events: multiply. GIVEN: restrict attention to cases where the condition holds, then ask how often the event happens there.
The prior is your belief before seeing evidence; the posterior is your updated belief after.

tex.t: P(\neg A) = 1 - P(A),\quad P(A\cup B) = P(A) + P(B),\quad P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B),\quad P(A \mid B) = \frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}

cards.title: Full joint probability table
cards.hook: List the probability of every possible world, then answer any question by adding rows.
formula: P(x₁) = sum of rows with x₁
cards.memory: Filter the rows, then add them up.
cards.trap: The table doesn't scale (2ⁿ) and is hard to specify: that motivates Bayesian networks.
explain: A full joint table lists the probability of EVERY complete combination of the variables. With it you can answer any question by adding the right rows.

To find P(X = x₁): keep the rows where X = x₁ and add them up (this 'sums out' the other variables). To estimate the table from experiments: probability = how often the event happened ÷ number of experiments.
The problem: n binary variables need 2ⁿ rows (5 → 32, 20 → over a million), which is too big to store or estimate.

tex.t: P(X = x) = \sum_y \sum_z P(X = x, Y = y, Z = z)

cards.hook: A Bayesian network stores only local tables P(node | parents) and multiplies them to get the full joint.
formula: X is a parent of Y
cards.memory: Parents point at children; each child only cares about its parents.
cards.trap: Must be a DAG (no cycles). Order variables causes-before-effects for a compact network.
explain: A Bayesian network stores the same information much more compactly. Each variable is a node; an arrow from X to Y means X directly influences Y. Each node only stores a small table: its probability given its parents.
To get the probability of a full combination, multiply each node's entry given its parents. Burglary: P(B)P(E)P(A|B,E)P(J|A)P(M|A).
For a 'false' value use 1 − the table entry (e.g. P(¬b) = 1 − 0.001 = 0.999).

cards.title: Bayes' rule: causal vs diagnostic
cards.hook: We usually know P(symptom | disease) but want P(disease | symptom).
formula: α makes the posterior sum to 1
cards.memory: Causal: Cause first in the condition. Diagnostic: Detective works backwards from clues.
cards.trap: P(S|D) ≠ P(D|S). A 90%-accurate test can still give a low posterior when the disease is rare.
explain: Bayes' rule lets you flip a conditional probability. Doctors know P(symptom | disease) (causal direction) but need P(disease | symptom) (diagnostic direction).
Multiply the likelihood P(S|D) by the prior P(D) and divide by how common the symptom is overall, P(S).
If the disease is rare, even a good test gives a modest posterior: most positives come from the many healthy people.

tex.t: P(D \mid S) = \frac{P(S \mid D)\,P(D)}{P(S)}, \qquad P(S) = P(S\mid D)P(D) + P(S \mid \neg D)P(\neg D)

where: normalisation constant (makes the posterior sum to 1)

tex.t: \text{Conditional independence: } P(X, Y \mid Z) = P(X \mid Z)\,P(Y \mid Z)

cards.title: Exact inference by enumeration
cards.hook: Sum over every possible value of the hidden variables, then normalise.
formula: filter j,m → group B/¬B → sum E,A → normalise
divide each score by s_B + s_¬B
cards.memory: Multiply along a path, add across branches, normalise at the end.
cards.trap: Unnormalised scores are NOT probabilities until divided by their total.
explain: Question: given John and Mary both called, what is the chance of a burglary? B is the query, J and M are the evidence, A and E are hidden (we don't know them, so we must consider every possibility).
Compute an unnormalised score for B = true: multiply the factors along each path of the tree and ADD over every value of E and A. Do the same for B = false.
Finally divide each score by their total so they sum to 1 (normalise). Lecture 11: s_B = 0.00059224, s_¬B = 0.00149186 → P(b | j, m) ≈ 0.284.
